summary: Provides a set of torture tests for Signaling Compression (SigComp) implementers. They check each Universal Decompressor Virtual Machine instruction in turn, especially boundary and error cases, and also test the dispatcher and state handler. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: A tough obstacle course for a program, built to catch mistakes in odd corner cases before real users hit them.

questions: how to test a sigcomp implementation
how do i test a sigcomp implementation
what boundary cases should a decompressor handle
subtitle: Comprehensive test cases for SigComp implementations, emphasizing boundary and error cases

tldr.problem: SigComp implementations must handle the Universal Decompressor Virtual Machine (UDVM), a dispatcher, and a state handler correctly, including edge cases that well-behaved compressors do not expose and that could be exploited by malicious messages.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC provides 'torture tests'—carefully crafted bytecode sequences that exercise each UDVM instruction in boundary conditions, test the dispatcher with unusual message patterns, and verify state handler behavior with multiple compartments, memory limits, and feedback.
tldr.outcome: Implementers can validate their SigComp stacks against comprehensive test vectors before deployment, increasing confidence that edge cases and attacks are handled safely.

today: RFC 4465 is an Informational RFC that documents comprehensive test vectors for SigComp implementations. These tests are used during development and validation of SigComp stacks to ensure correctness before deployment in production networks.

sections.title: What Are Torture Tests
sections.content:
A torture test is a carefully constructed piece of code or data designed to expose bugs by exercising boundary conditions and error cases that normal operations do not encounter. This RFC provides torture tests for SigComp implementations.

Unlike the SigComp Users' Guide (RFC 4464), which documents how to implement algorithms correctly, these tests focus on cases that might break an implementation: numeric overflow, division by zero, instructions that overwrite themselves, memory regions that wrap around, and state transitions that exceed normal limits.

Each test includes the expected output, the number of UDVM cycles that execution should consume, and notes on which specific boundary conditions are being checked. Tests are provided in both human-readable assembly language and raw UDVM bytecode.
sections.plainLanguage: Torture tests are like a tough workout routine for a SigComp program. They test weird corner cases that a normal program wouldn't hit, so you can make sure it handles them correctly and doesn't crash.

sections.title: Tests for UDVM Instructions
sections.content:
The RFC organizes UDVM instruction tests by functional category:

Bit and Arithmetic Operations: Tests for AND, OR, NOT, LSHIFT, RSHIFT (bit manipulation); ADD, SUBTRACT, MULTIPLY, DIVIDE, REMAINDER (arithmetic). Boundary cases include overflow, zero results, and cases where the instruction overwrites its own operands.

Data Movement: Tests for LOAD, MULTILOAD, COPY, COPY-LITERAL, COPY-OFFSET, and MEMSET. Checks whether instructions correctly handle circular buffer wrapping, byte-by-byte copying semantics, and overwriting of the instruction itself or the buffer registers.

Input Instructions: Tests for INPUT-BITS, INPUT-HUFFMAN, and INPUT-BYTES. Verifies correct handling of bit ordering, zero-bit reads, and requests for data beyond message end.

Special Operations: Tests for SORT-ASCENDING, SORT-DESCENDING, CRC, and SHA-1. Checks correct hashing, CRC polynomial calculation, and stable sorting of equal-valued items.

Control Flow: Tests for JUMP, COMPARE, and stack operations. Verifies label resolution, conditional jumps, and stack manipulation boundary cases.

State Operations: Tests for STATE-CREATE and STATE-ACCESS. Validates state memory allocation and shared state access.
sections.plainLanguage: There are tests for moving bits, doing math, copying data, reading from messages, calculating checksums, jumping around, and managing saved state. Each test tries something weird to see if the computer handles it right.

sections.title: Tests for the Dispatcher and State Handler
sections.content:
Dispatcher Tests exercise the component that routes compressed messages and manages cycles:

  • Message-based transport: Tests handling of complete SigComp messages that fit within a single packet or datagram.
  • Stream-based transport: Tests handling of messages split across multiple packets, requiring reassembly.
  • Cycles checking: Verifies that the dispatcher correctly accounts for UDVM cycle consumption and enforces the minimum cycles-per-bit limit.
  • Input past end of message: Tests boundary cases when bytecode tries to read beyond the end of the compressed data.

State Handler Tests exercise the component that manages saved decompression state:

  • Feedback mechanism: Tests the return of state identifiers via the feedback channel when a message is successfully decompressed and saved.
  • State memory management: Tests creation and eviction of state items when memory limits are reached.
  • Multiple compartments: Tests isolation of state across different protocol flows or sessions.
  • Bytecode state creation: Tests the END-MESSAGE instruction and its parameters for saving state.
sections.plainLanguage: The dispatcher passes messages to the decompressor and counts cycles. The state handler saves and loads decompressed messages between messages. These tests check both work right with weird message patterns and memory limits.

sections.title: Running the Tests
sections.content:
Each test section in the RFC provides:

  • Assembly language code: Written in the UDVM assembly language defined in RFC 4464, readable and annotatable.
  • Raw bytecode: In Appendix A, provided for implementers who wish to run the test directly without assembling.
  • Expected output: The exact byte sequence or message the decompressor should produce when the test runs successfully.
  • Cycle count: The number of UDVM cycles the test should consume, used to verify that the implementation's cycle accounting is correct.
  • Boundary cases covered: Comments explaining what edge cases the test exercises and why they matter.

Implementers should run each test with their SigComp implementation and verify that the output and cycle count match. Any deviation suggests a bug in handling boundary conditions. Some tests include multiple test cases that vary by input (e.g., triggering different error paths), and should all be exercised.
sections.plainLanguage: Each test shows you the code, what it should output, how many CPU cycles it should take, and what weird corner case it checks. Run it on your code and see if you get the right answer.

sections.title: Coverage and Validation Strategy
sections.content:
The RFC covers the minimum decompression memory size (2K), minimum state memory size (2K), and minimum cycles per bit (16), ensuring tests run on the smallest compliant implementations.

Not every possible combination of instructions and parameters is tested; instead, tests focus on:

  • Individual instruction behavior: Does each UDVM instruction handle its parameters and memory correctly?
  • Boundary cases: Wrap-around, overflow, zero values, division by zero, and self-overwriting code.
  • Transport edge cases: Message reassembly, cycle limits, and end-of-data scenarios.
  • State transitions: Creation, retrieval, eviction, and multi-compartment isolation.

The tests do not attempt to verify correct operation of specific compression algorithms; that is covered in RFC 4464. Instead, they validate the virtual machine and state management infrastructure that any compression algorithm relies on.
sections.plainLanguage: The tests do not cover every possible combination, but they hit all the tricky corners—overflow, wrapping memory, division by zero, and state management. If you pass these, your implementation is probably solid.
